paper.title: Robots That Ask For Help: Uncertainty Alignment for Large Language Model Planners
paper.central_claim: KnowNo reformulates language planning as multiple-choice QA and uses conformal prediction to provide user-specified statistical task-completion guarantees while minimizing human help, in single- and multi-step embodied tasks.
paper.scope_decision: in_scope (pending full review): conformal calibration of an LLM planner's options with human hand-back on robot tasks.

evidence.quote: KnowNo builds on the theory of conformal prediction to provide statistical guarantees on task completion while minimizing human help in complex multi-step planning settings

Prior work in language-based planning either does not seek such clarifications [ 1 ] or does so via extensive prompting [ 2 ] , which requires careful prompt engineering to prevent the robot from excessively relying on seeking assistance.
We collectively refer to these sufficiency and minimality conditions as uncertainty alignment .
evidence.support_explanation: Formalized desiderata: calibrated confidence and minimal help.

evidence.quote: This eliminates plans that the LLM considers unlikely and reduces the problem of next-step prediction down to a single next-token prediction
Otherwise, we deem the LLM uncertain over possible actions and trigger human help.
evidence.support_explanation: Decision rule: non-singleton set -> ask human.

evidence.quote: Here, we present a novel extension of CP to multi-step settings that tackles this challenge.
Thus, the i.i.d. assumption for the coverage guarantee is no longer valid.
The proof immediately follows from the fact that under the assumption of accurate human help, the robot fails only when the prediction set does not contain the true label
evidence.support_explanation: Guarantee is about plan-level coverage given faithful human help.

evidence.quote: Labeling the calibration data takes about 4 hours (for 400 examples) in the multi-step setting and 1.5 hours in single-step settings.
For experiments here, we assume that the human faithfully provides help.
200 trials are run for each method/setting.
Then we run 50 trials for both methods in hardware.

evidence.support_explanation: Hardware multi-step results at matched plan success.
Mobile manipulation: plan 0.87 vs task 0.76; help 0.67 vs 0.81; trial count not in main text.

evidence.quote: Plan success rate is fixed between KnowNo and Simple Set for comparing the other metrics.
Table 1 shows that KnowNo reduces the human help rate by 14% step-wise and 8% trial-wise, while also reducing the average prediction set size.

The primary limitation of our work is that the task completion guarantee assumes environments (objects) are fully grounded in the text input to the LLM, and the actions proposed by the LLM planner can be executed successfully.
Another limitation is that, for the task guarantee to hold, the human needs to faithfully provide help when the robot needs it.
Ensemble Set can perform well but is computationally expensive.
we find that it exhibits significant MCQA bias towards options D and E and against A and B, affecting the overall performance.
evidence.support_explanation: GPT-3.5 variant biased; guarantee still met.

evidence.quote: To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to employ CP for language-based planning.
